lessons.title: Writing and simplifying ratios
lessons.summary: Write an ordered ratio, use matching units and simplify every term.
lessons.objective: Write an ordered ratio, use matching units and simplify every term.
lessons.before: Check that you can multiply and divide whole numbers.
lessons.ideas:
Divide both terms by the same common factor. The first term still refers to the first thing named.

Match units before simplifying. One metre is 100 centimetres.

Apply the same division to every term.
lessons.method:
Why does the order matter?

A ratio says how many parts of one thing correspond to parts of another. Read the names in order before assigning the numbers.

What if the units are different?

First express both measurements in centimetres, or both in metres. This makes one unit on the left represent the same length as one unit on the right.

What if there are three quantities?

Find a factor that divides all three counts. Draw three rows of part boxes to keep the terms in order.
mistakes: Swapping the terms changes what each number describes.
Changing only the unit name does not change the number of units.
A factor shared by just two terms is not sufficient.

examples.title: Simplify a ratio in the original order
examples.question: Write \(20:25\) in its simplest form.
examples.solution:
Divide both terms by their highest common factor, 5.

The numbers stay in their original order to give \(4:5\).

examples.title: Use one unit before comparing
examples.question: Two rolls measure 15 m and 1800 cm. Give the ratio of their lengths in simplest form in that order.
examples.solution:
Convert the first roll to 1500 cm. Both values now use centimetres.

Divide both parts by 300 to get \(5:6\).

examples.title: Simplify three terms together
examples.question: Three bins hold 54, 63 and 81 tiles. Give the ratio of their quantities in simplest form in that order.
examples.solution:
The three counts have common factor 9.

Divide every count by that factor: \(6:7:9\).

lessons.title: Sharing in a ratio
lessons.summary: Find one part from the total, from one share or from the difference.
lessons.objective: Find one part from the total, from one share or from the difference.
lessons.before: Check that you can multiply and divide whole numbers.
lessons.ideas:
Add the terms. Divide the total by that sum. Multiply by the number of parts in the wanted share.

Use the known person's part count to find the value of one part.

Subtract the terms to find how many parts the difference represents.
lessons.method:
How can I split a total fairly?

Draw one box for each part. The whole amount fills all the boxes. The equal boxes represent equal amounts.

What if one share is known?

Circle only the boxes for the person or group whose share is given. Divide that share by the number of boxes you circled.

What if the difference is given?

Draw the two rows from the same starting point. The extra boxes in the longer row show what the difference is worth.
mistakes: The values in the ratio count parts. They are not the amounts being shared.
Adding the two terms would divide by the total part count, which belongs to the whole amount.
The difference between amounts does not tell you the total share.

examples.title: Share the whole between two groups
examples.question: A workshop shares 99 tiles between Art and Design in the ratio \(4:7\). How many tiles does Design receive?
examples.solution:
There are 11 equal parts. Divide the total, 99, by 11 to find 9 tiles per part.

Design has 7 parts. Multiply 7 by 9.

The answer is \(63\).

examples.title: Use a single known share
examples.question: Two teams collect cans in the ratio Red to Blue \(6:7\). Red collects 54 cans. How many does Blue collect?
examples.solution:
The known 54 cans correspond to 6 parts. That makes 9 cans per part.

Blue gets 7 of those equal parts.

The answer is \(63\).

examples.title: Use a known difference
examples.question: Inez and Lee save money in the ratio \(7:9\). Lee has £18 more than Inez. How much do they have together, in pounds?
examples.solution:
The difference in shares is \(9-7=2\) parts. Divide £18 by 2 to get £9 for one part.

Together they have 16 parts of £9 each.

The answer is \(144\).

lessons.title: Recipes and map scales
lessons.summary: Scale quantities using the unitary method and move between map lengths and real distances.
lessons.objective: Scale quantities using the unitary method and move between map lengths and real distances.
lessons.before: Check that you can multiply and divide whole numbers.
lessons.ideas:
Work down to one, then scale up to the new number of servings.

A scale \(1:40000\) means 1 map centimetre represents 40,000 ground centimetres, or 400 m.

Divide the real distance by the real length represented by one map centimetre.
lessons.method:
How do I scale an ingredient?

Divide by the starting number of servings. The amount for one serving is the bridge to any other serving size.

How do I read a map scale?

One unit on the map represents several of the same units on the ground. First choose centimetres so that the map and real units match.

How do I get back to a length on the map?

Find the ground distance that corresponds to one map centimetre. Count how many such units the full distance contains.
mistakes: Changing the servings by two does not mean adding two grams.
Convert to the requested unit after applying the scale.
Use matching units in the division. Metres and centimetres cannot be divided as if they were the same unit.

examples.title: Adapt a recipe to a new serving size
examples.question: A recipe for 6 people uses 240 g of rice. How much rice is needed for 10 people at the same serving size?
examples.solution:
Divide the starting amount by 6 to find 40 g per person.

For 10 people, use 10 of those servings.

The answer is \(400\).

examples.title: Turn a map length into a ground distance
examples.question: On a map with scale \(1:50000\), a paved route is 6 cm long. What is its real length in metres?
examples.solution:
6 map centimetres represent \(6\times 50000\) real centimetres.

Divide 300000 real centimetres by 100 to turn them into metres.

The answer is \(3000\).

examples.title: Work back from a real distance to a map length
examples.question: A pathway is 4200 m long. On a plan drawn at \(1:60000\), how many centimetres long is the pathway?
examples.solution:
One map centimetre represents 60000 cm on the ground, or 600 m.

Find how many of those ground-distance units fit in 4200 m.

The answer is \(7\).

lessons.title: Unit prices and best value
lessons.summary: Compare prices using the cost per item or per unit and recognise equal value.
lessons.objective: Compare prices using the cost per item or per unit and recognise equal value.
lessons.before: Check that you can multiply and divide whole numbers.
lessons.ideas:
Divide price by quantity. Keep track of the price unit and the quantity unit.

Find the price per unit for both packs and choose the lower one.

Choose equal value when the two unit costs match exactly.
lessons.method:
What does per item mean?

A price per item tells you the cost of one equal item. The same idea works per metre, per kilogram or per litre.

Which pack gives better value?

Compare packs by pricing the same unit. A large pack can be cheaper per unit even if its total price is higher.

Can two packs offer the same value?

If the quantities and prices grow by the same factor, the unit price stays the same. Checking the two unit prices makes this visible.
mistakes: Use the full number of items even when the pack contains several groups.
Compare pence with pence and metres with metres.
A higher price for a larger pack does not settle the question on its own.

examples.title: Find the price for one item
examples.question: A bag of 8 seed packets costs 208 p. Find the cost of one seed packet in pence.
examples.solution:
The total price 208 p buys 8 packets.

Divide 208 by 8.

The answer is \(26\).

examples.title: Compare prices fairly
examples.question: Pack A contains 8 metres of cord and costs 248 p. Pack B contains 15 metres and costs 525 p. Decide which pack gives better value, or show that they give the same value.
examples.solution:
Compare the cost of the same amount, for example one metre.

Pack A costs \(248\div 8=31\) p per metre. Pack B costs \(525\div 15=35\) p per metre.

Answer: Pack A.

examples.title: Compare prices fairly
examples.question: Pack A contains 9 metres of cord and costs 288 p. Pack B contains 16 metres and costs 512 p. Decide which pack gives better value, or show that they give the same value.
examples.solution:
Compare the cost of the same amount, for example one metre.

Pack A costs \(288\div 9=32\) p per metre. Pack B costs \(512\div 16=32\) p per metre.

Answer: They give the same value.
